title: Notation
intro: Western music is written on a five-line staff: vertical position shows pitch and the shape of each note shows its length. This page covers the pitch side: staff, clefs, note names, accidentals and how they map to the keyboard.

blocks.text: The keyboard and the note names

Pitches are named with the letters A to G, repeating every octave. On a piano the white keys are the natural notes C D E F G A B; the black keys sit between them, in groups of two and three. C is the white key just left of each group of two black keys.

Between most neighbouring white keys there is a black key, so they are two semitones apart (a whole tone). E–F and B–C have no black key between them: they are one semitone (a half step) apart. This pattern of tones and semitones is the backbone of the major scale.

examples.label: C D E F G A B C (white keys)

items: ♯ sharp: one semitone higher. F♯ is the black key just above F.
♭ flat: one semitone lower. B♭ is the black key just below B.
♮ natural: cancels a sharp or flat.
𝄪 double sharp and 𝄫 double flat: two semitones up or down. F𝄪 sounds like G.
An accidental lasts until the end of the bar (measure) and applies only to that line or space and octave. A key signature, at the start of each line, applies throughout.

blocks.text: Different names for the same key are enharmonic equivalents: F♯ and G♭, B and C♭, E♯ and F. They sound the same on a piano, but they are not interchangeable on paper. The spelling shows the note's role: in D major the third is F♯ (a kind of F, so the scale uses each letter once); in D♭ major the fourth is G♭. Choosing the right spelling is part of reading harmony.

The staff has five lines and four spaces. Each line and space is one letter name; going up one position goes up one letter. Ledger lines extend the staff above or below. A clef at the start fixes which line is which note:

blocks.alt: Two five-line staves. On the treble staff the lines from bottom to top are E4, G4, B4, D5 and F5 and the spaces F4, A4, C5 and E5. On the bass staff the lines are G2, B2, D3, F3 and A3 and the spaces A2, C3, E3 and G3. Middle C sits on a ledger line between the staves.
blocks.caption: The treble (G) clef and bass (F) clef, with the note on each line and space. Middle C (C4) sits on one ledger line below the treble staff or one above the bass staff.

items: Treble clef (G clef): its curl circles the second line, G4. Lines from the bottom: E G B D F ('Every Good Boy Does Fine'); spaces F A C E.
Bass clef (F clef): its two dots surround the fourth line, F3. Lines from the bottom: G B D F A ('Good Boys Do Fine Always'); spaces A C E G ('All Cows Eat Grass').
Alto clef (C clef on the middle line, C4): used for viola. Tenor clef (C clef on the fourth line): used for the high range of cello, bassoon and trombone.
The grand staff joins a treble and a bass staff with a brace, as in piano music. Middle C lies exactly between them.

blocks.text: Scientific pitch notation numbers each octave from C: C4 is middle C, B3 the note just below it, C5 the next C up. The lowest piano key is A0 and the highest C8. Older books use Helmholtz names (c′ for middle C, C, for C1), and some MIDI software calls middle C 'C3'; always check which convention a source uses.

blocks.title: Read the line
blocks.text: In treble clef, which note sits on the middle (third) line? And in bass clef?
solution: Treble lines from the bottom are E G B D F, so the middle line is B4. Bass lines are G B D F A, so the middle line is D3.
blocks.answer: B4 in treble, D3 in bass

blocks.title: Enharmonics
blocks.text: Give an enharmonic spelling of each: C♯, F♭, B♯, E𝄫.
solution: C♯ = D♭; F♭ = E; B♯ = C (one octave up: B♯3 = C4); E𝄫 = D.

blocks.title: Semitones
blocks.text: How many semitones are there from E4 up to C5? Count the keys.

Sources: Gould, E. (2011). Behind Bars: The Definitive Guide to Music Notation. Faber Music; Kostka, S., Payne, D. & Almén, B. (2018). Tonal Harmony, 8th ed. McGraw-Hill; Gotham, M. et al. (2021). Open Music Theory, version 2 (viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory).
